report.source_text: After returning from the CT scan, the patient’s condition deteriorated within minutes. The oxygen saturation dropped to about 70% and did not recover even with 10 L of O2 administered via reservoir mask. Respiratory exhaustion was imminent. While intravenous Solu-Medrol and Co-Amoxicillin were administered, intubation was initiated, which proved to be extremely difficult due to swelling of the supraglottic soft tissue, although video-guided GlideScope was used. Consequently, the patient went into hypoxaemia and eventually into cardiac arrest. Reanimation protocol was immediately initiated. After even direct tracheal airway access failed, another attempt was made to orally intubate the patient, this time with success. After around 5 min of mechanical reanimation and a total of 2 mg intravenous adrenalin, ROSC was achieved.

clinician.final_diagnosis: epiglottitis/supraglottitis due to infection with N. meningitidis
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 78-year-old woman presented with throat pain, hoarseness, painful submandibular swelling, coughing, dysphagia, and breathing difficulties. Initial clinical examination confirmed submandibular swelling, restricted mouth opening, and ruled out meningism. Blood cultures revealed N. meningitidis bacteraemia. Neck CT showed the thumbprint sign of acute epiglottitis and supraglottic swelling causing airway stenosis. The patient deteriorated rapidly after CT with hypoxia, difficult intubation, cardiac arrest, and successful resuscitation. She remained intubated for a week, with follow-up CT showing decreased epiglottis swelling. Antibiotic therapy was adjusted from Co-Amoxicillin to ceftriaxone targeting N. meningitidis. The patient improved, ventilation was ceased, and tracheostomy reversed. She was discharged to neurorehabilitation for sequelae from hypoxic injury.
